Step zero · setting up a repo
Two ways to start working with a repo
Start something new
Create, then publish
publish
  1. GitHub Desktop: File → New repository. Name it, tick “Initialize with a README”.
  2. Click Publish repository. Now it’s on GitHub too.
  3. On github.com, invite your team: Settings → Collaborators.
Join something that exists
Clone it
clone
  1. Accept the invite on github.com.
  2. GitHub Desktop: File → Clone repository, pick it from the list.
  3. Choose where the folder lives on your computer.
Either way: a copy on your computer, linked to GitHub.

Command 2 of 6 · Local only
status: what has changed?
git status
modified: skills/error-copy/SKILL.md
Local only · safe anytime
What it does
Lists the files you’ve changed, added or deleted since your last commit. It changes nothing.
In GitHub Desktop
The Changes tab on the left. It updates by itself.
Think of it as
The dot on a file tab that tells you there are unsaved changes.

Local only · not shared yet
What it does
Saves the staged changes as a snapshot with a short message, in your local repo.
In GitHub Desktop

push: send your save points to GitHub
git push

Local → Remote · now it’s shared
What it does
Uploads your new commits to GitHub. Until you push, they only exist on your machine.
In GitHub Desktop
Push origin. On a new branch, the button says Publish branch.

Block 5 · 14:10–14:35 · Together, one click at a time
Branch, commit, push
1
Current branch → New branch. Name it your-name/skill-name.
2
Changes tab: your file is ticked. That’s staged.
3
Summary “Add error copy skill”, then Commit to your branch.
4
Publish branch. Your commit is now on GitHub.
5
Open the repo on github.com and find your branch.
Bonus: change one line, commit and push again. History now shows two save points.
Stopping and starting
Pick up exactly where you left off
Before you stop
  1. Commit what you have, even if unfinished: “WIP: steps 1–3 of error copy skill”.
  2. Push. Your work is now safe on GitHub, and you can continue from any computer.
  3. Write what’s next in the commit message or the pull request.
When you come back
  1. Open GitHub Desktop and check that Current branch is yours.
  2. Click Fetch origin, then Pull if anything new came in.
  3. PR merged meanwhile? Switch to main, pull, and make a new branch.
Closing the laptop loses nothing. But uncommitted work exists on that one computer only.
14:35 · Break
Back at 14:40
This break is also practice: you’ll stop, then pick up where you left off.
Before you go
Check GitHub Desktop says No local changes. Then quit GitHub Desktop and VS Code completely.
When you’re back
Reopen, check your branch, Fetch origin. Move your sticky to Resumed.
Remote only · lives on GitHub, not in Git
Pull request: ask to merge your branch
1
Open
Create Pull Request in GitHub Desktop. Describe what you changed.
2
Review
A teammate comments. You fix, commit and push; the PR updates itself.
3
Merge
After approval, the branch joins main on GitHub.
Merging happens on GitHub, so your computer is now behind. Switch to main and pull to catch up.

Command 6 of 6 · Remote → Local
pull: bring the team’s changes to you
git pull
pull = git fetch + git merge
Remote → Local · do it first
What it does
Downloads new commits from GitHub and merges them into your files.
In GitHub Desktop
Fetch origin only checks for news. Pull origin brings it into your files.
Think of it as
Checking the studio wall for what others pinned up since you last looked.

Preview · more in session 3
Merge conflict: when two people change the same line
Three mix-ups everyone makes
“Where did my change go?”
“I committed, but my colleague can’t see it.”
A commit is local. Push to share it.
“I fetched, but my files didn’t change.”
Fetch only looks. Pull brings changes into your files.
“I pushed, but it’s not on main.”
It’s on your branch. It reaches main when the pull request is merged.
When in doubt: open the Changes and History tabs in GitHub Desktop. That’s git status and git log.
